target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday removes the main scheduling barrier to voting and therefore makes voting easier for everyone.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably give people time off to vote, because private employers are not required to provide paid leave. Low-income retail and service workers may still have to work or take unpaid time, so the scheduling barrier is not actually solved for the people most affected.

target: AG1’s reliance on a national holiday as an effective way to increase turnout.
objection: Research and experience suggest that changing the calendar by itself is usually not an effective turnout strategy compared with direct voting-access reforms such as employer-mandated time off to vote, expanded early voting, mail voting, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s update that a holiday should be paired with enforceable paid voting time, implying the holiday still has independent value.
objection: If lawmakers are going to mandate paid voting time anyway, the national holiday becomes largely redundant; the decisive reform is the enforceable time-to-vote rule, not the calendar change.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday adds value by reducing friction, eliminating the need for special requests, helping childcare logistics, and symbolically elevating civic participation.
objection: Those benefits either depend on the holiday being paired with enforceable protections or are better achieved by direct access reforms. Symbolic and logistical benefits do not overcome the fact that a holiday alone still fails to guarantee paid, usable time for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday would create a fairer, more effective package when combined with time-to-vote protections.
objection: Even with that package, a holiday remains a mis-targeted policy because the day off primarily helps workers with flexible jobs, while low-income workers can still be scheduled to work or lose income, making the policy potentially less equitable than direct access reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday creates a uniform nationwide baseline and makes time-to-vote protections easier to implement.
objection: The core equity problem remains: federal holiday status does not require paid time off from private employers, so the workers who most need voting access can still be forced to work or lose wages. That means a holiday can be secondary or even inequitable compared with enforceable voting-access rules.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday adds a uniform national benefit beyond state-by-state access reforms.
objection: If enforceable time-to-vote rules are already in place, the holiday is not the causal lever; the enforceable rules are. A national holiday then mainly adds political and implementation overhead without solving the paid-time problem for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that many workplaces will close or reduce schedules because Election Day is a federal holiday, giving workers real schedule relief.
objection: That is unreliable because closures are discretionary, and the sectors where low-income and shift workers are concentrated often stay open. So the holiday does not reliably deliver the schedule relief AG1 claims.

target: AG1’s reliance on international precedent to support a national holiday.
objection: The fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays does not prove that a U.S. federal holiday would work the same way, because the U.S. still depends on enforceable paid time off and labor rules that make the holiday meaningful.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday is useful because it reduces the need for workers to navigate or claim leave.
objection: That uncertainty can be eliminated directly by enforceable time-to-vote laws that make voting leave automatic, paid, and protected from employer discretion. In that design, a holiday is unnecessary for removing leave-navigation burdens.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday is simpler and reduces operational complexity compared with time-to-vote enforcement.
objection: A holiday is not a complete solution, because the real workplace problem still has to be addressed through additional rules. If the goal is paid, equitable voting time, those enforceable protections are what matter, and the holiday just adds another legislative layer without guaranteeing the outcome.

target: AG1’s view that a holiday is a useful front-line scheduling fix even if paid voting leave is also needed.
objection: A federal holiday does not legally require private employers to give low-income hourly or shift workers paid time to vote, so centering the holiday still fails to solve the key reliability problem for the workers most constrained by schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces leave-navigation burdens and makes time-to-vote enforcement easier to administer.
objection: The same benefits can be built directly into enforceable time-to-vote statutes by making leave automatic, paid, and protected for covered workers, without needing a national holiday at all.

target: AG1’s suggestion that centering the holiday helps build the coalition and momentum needed for the rest of the reforms.
objection: That is speculative, because a holiday does not ensure the enforceable protections will actually be passed or designed to cover shift workers. It may instead consume political capital and delay the measures that directly solve wage-loss and scheduling problems.
